subject: chem
title: Atomic Structure
subtitle: Protons, neutrons, electrons, isotopes and mass spectrometry.
concept: Atoms consist of a dense positive nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons arranged in shells and subshells. The number of protons (atomic number) defines the element.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. They have identical chemical properties but different masses.
Mass spectrometry measures relative atomic mass by ionising atoms, accelerating them through a magnetic field, and detecting relative abundance at each m/z value.

notes.heading: Subatomic Particles
items: Atoms consist of a dense positive nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons in shells. The atomic number (Z) = number of protons; it defines the element. The mass number (A) = protons + neutrons.
Proton: relative mass 1, charge +1. Neutron: relative mass 1, charge 0. Electron: relative mass ≈ 1/1836 (negligible), charge −1.

notes.heading: Electron Configuration and Subshells
items: Electrons occupy shells divided into subshells: s (max 2), p (max 6), d (max 10), f (max 14). The order of filling is: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p.

Hund's rule: electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly before pairing. Copper and chromium are anomalous — the extra stability of a half-filled (3d⁵) or fully filled (3d¹⁰) d subshell means one electron moves from 4s: Cr = [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹; Cu = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹.
When forming ions, electrons are always removed from the highest principal quantum number first — remove 4s before 3d in transition metals: Fe²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁶.

notes.heading: Isotopes and Relative Atomic Mass
items: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same Z) with different mass numbers (different number of neutrons). They have identical chemical properties but different physical properties (mass).
Relative atomic mass (Aᵣ): weighted mean mass of an atom relative to 1/12 the mass of ¹²C. Aᵣ = Σ(isotope mass × fractional abundance). Not necessarily a whole number.

notes.heading: Mass Spectrometry
items: Four stages: ionisation (electron bombardment removes one electron → M⁺ cation) → acceleration (electric field) → deflection (magnetic field — lighter ions and those with higher charge deflect more) → detection.

The x-axis of the mass spectrum is m/z (mass-to-charge ratio). The molecular ion peak (M⁺) at the highest m/z gives the relative molecular mass. Fragment peaks arise from bond cleavage. The tallest peak (base peak) is the most abundant fragment.
Isotope patterns: chlorine (³⁵Cl : ³⁷Cl ≈ 3:1) gives M and M+2 peaks in a 3:1 ratio; bromine (≈1:1) gives equal M and M+2 peaks.

notes.heading: Ionisation Energies
items: First ionisation energy (IE₁): X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻. It increases across a period (more protons, same shielding) with two dips: Al < Mg (3p electron easier to remove than 3s) and S < P (paired 3p electron repelled by its partner).
Successive ionisation energies increase steadily, then show a large jump when an electron is removed from a new, inner shell — this reveals the group of the element.

definitions.body: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The weighted mean mass of an atom of an element relative to 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
The energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms: X(g) → X+(g) + e−.

workedExamples.q: Chlorine has two isotopes: Cl-35 (75.0%) and Cl-37 (25.0%). Calculate the relative atomic mass.
Write the full electron configuration of Fe2+.

mistakes: Removing electrons from 3d instead of 4s when forming transition metal ions.
Confusing mass number with relative atomic mass (Ar is a weighted average, not a whole number).
Forgetting Cu and Cr have anomalous configurations due to extra stability of half-filled/full 3d.
tips: In mass spectrometry questions, the tallest peak is the most abundant isotope — not necessarily the heaviest.
Always state the equation for first ionisation energy: X(g) → X+(g) + e−.
Successive ionisation energy data: a big jump between nth and (n+1)th IE means the element is in Group n.

flashcards.q: What is the charge and mass of a proton?
What is the formula for relative atomic mass?
Why do Cr and Cu have anomalous electron configurations?
flashcards.a: Half-filled (3d⁵) and fully-filled (3d¹⁰) subshells have extra stability, so one electron moves from 4s to 3d.

flashcards.q: What are the four stages of mass spectrometry?
flashcards.a: Ionisation → acceleration → deflection in magnetic field → detection.
Energy to remove 1 mole of electrons from 1 mole of gaseous atoms: X(g) → X+(g) + e−.

flashcards.q: What does a large jump in successive ionisation energies indicate?
flashcards.a: The electron being removed is from a new, inner shell — reveals the group of the element.

questions.q: Bromine has isotopes Br-79 (50.7%) and Br-81 (49.3%). What is the Ar?
What is the electron configuration of Cu (Z=29)?
questions.exp: Cu is anomalous: fully filled 3d10 with 4s1 is more stable than 3d9 4s2.

questions.q: In mass spectrometry, which ions are deflected most in the magnetic field?
questions.exp: Deflection increases with charge and decreases with mass — light, highly charged ions deflect most.

questions.q: What does the molecular ion peak (M+) represent?
opts: The parent molecule minus one electron
questions.exp: M+ is the intact molecule that has lost one electron during ionisation — it appears at the highest m/z.

recall: State the relative mass and charge of a proton, neutron and electron.
Write the electron configuration of Fe²⁺.

Calculate Ar given two isotopes and their abundances.
Describe the four stages of a mass spectrometer.
